question: Reading the nbtree README, an engineer notices that PostgreSQL takes a short read lock on each B-tree page while examining it, and concludes that the Lehman & Yao design buys nothing over classic lock coupling — so the team can stop reasoning about splits during descent altogether. Where does that reasoning go wrong?
choices: The short per-page lock is lock coupling under another name. What actually protects descending readers is that a split takes an exclusive lock on the entire tree level while it runs, so no reader can ever observe a half-finished split

Those locks are taken only on internal pages; leaf pages are examined with no lock at all, which is where the Lehman & Yao guarantee lives. The high key and right-link exist purely to support backward (ORDER BY … DESC) scans

Coupling means holding the parent's lock until the child's has been acquired, which serialises every descent near the root — and PostgreSQL never does that. The per-page lock exists only because backends share one buffer pool, so a page can change while being examined; Lehman & Yao assumed each process read a private copy. The lock is dropped before the next level, so a reader can still land on a page that split under it, and the high key plus right-link is exactly what lets it detect that and move right on its own

The lock is a concession to page deletion, which Lehman & Yao did not support: without it a reader could follow a right-link into a page that was concurrently unlinked. Splits themselves are handled by re-descending from the root whenever the high key check fails
explanation: The failure mode B-link solves is not slowness but wrongness: a reader picks a downlink for key 55, a writer splits that leaf before the reader arrives, and 55 has already moved to a new right sibling the parent does not point at yet — the reader reports a row that exists as missing. The classic cure, lock coupling, holds the parent's lock until the child's is acquired so no split can slip into the gap; it is correct but turns the top of the tree into a contention point, since every single descent passes through the root. Lehman & Yao's contribution was to make the split survivable rather than invisible: the right-link and the high key let a reader that landed on a stale page notice (my key exceeds this page's high key) and repair itself by moving right, with no lock held across levels. PostgreSQL's short per-page lock does not reintroduce coupling — it is a separate concern created by the shared buffer pool, where a page can be modified while a backend is reading it, which the original algorithm never had to handle because it assumed private page copies. The distractors each misplace the mechanism: a level-wide exclusive lock during splits would be a far worse bottleneck than the coupling being avoided; leaves are examined under the same brief lock and left-links are PostgreSQL's addition for DESC scans, not the seat of the guarantee; and page deletion is genuinely a PostgreSQL deviation (only empty pages, two-staged through half-dead) but it is not why the read lock exists, and re-descending from the root would throw away the move-right property that makes the design cheap.

question: A `users` table carries six indexes, none of them on `last_login`, and `pg_stat_all_tables` shows `n_tup_hot_upd` nearly equal to `n_tup_upd`. A new screen needs 'users active this week', so a developer adds a seventh index, on `last_login` — the column every login UPDATE touches. Write throughput on the table collapses, and both table and index bloat climb. What happened?
choices: The login UPDATE now changes an indexed column, so it no longer qualifies as a HOT update. Those updates used to touch zero indexes; each one now inserts an entry into all seven and leaves seven future-dead entries for VACUUM. The cost is not the seventh index in isolation — it is the loss of the HOT discount on the table's dominant write

The new index's shape is the bottleneck: `last_login` is monotonically increasing, so every insert lands on the rightmost leaf, and the resulting stream of page splits at the right edge serialises the writers

Seven indexes instead of six is one extra index insert per update, roughly 17% more index work. The collapse must come from the new index being unvacuumed; once autovacuum has processed it once, throughput returns to its previous level
Each login UPDATE now clears the visibility-map bit on the heap page, so index-only scans through the other six indexes degrade into heap fetches, and that extra read I/O starves the writers
explanation: A HOT update needs two things: no column used by any index changed, and the new version fits on the same heap page. When both hold, no index is touched at all — the index keeps pointing at the original line pointer, which becomes a redirect into the HOT chain. This table was getting that discount on nearly every update, which is exactly what `n_tup_hot_upd` ≈ `n_tup_upd` reports. Indexing `last_login` breaks the first condition for precisely the write that dominates the workload, so the table flips from 'zero index writes per update' to 'seven index inserts per update, plus seven dead entries', and VACUUM must now scan all seven indexes to collect them. That is the standing write amplification the Sheet describes, switched on in one DDL statement. The judgement call is whether the query is worth it: a partial index does not rescue HOT (the column still counts as indexed regardless of the predicate), and lowering `fillfactor` only helps the same-page condition, not the changed-column one — so the real options are to serve the screen another way, accept the tax, or move the churning column out of the table. The distractors are each a real phenomenon aimed at the wrong target: monotonically increasing keys are the cheap case for a B-tree, since rightmost-page splits are sequential and PostgreSQL has fast-path handling for them; the 17% arithmetic assumes a baseline of six index writes per update when the baseline was zero; and the visibility-map bit is cleared by any write to the page, HOT updates included, so it cannot explain a change that began with the new index.

question: A reporting query is served by `CREATE INDEX ON events (tenant_id) INCLUDE (amount)`. On a staging copy restored from a dump, `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` shows `Index Only Scan … Heap Fetches: 0` in well under a millisecond. In production — same plan node, same row count — the same query takes 400 ms with `Heap Fetches` almost equal to rows returned. Production is written to continuously. What is the diagnosis?
choices: INCLUDE payload does not survive leaf splits: the split truncates non-key attributes, so on an index that has grown and split many times, `amount` has to be re-read from the heap
The production index is bloated, so its tree has more levels and each descent costs extra page reads; `EXPLAIN` attributes those extra reads to `Heap Fetches`
Planner statistics on the production table are stale, so the row estimate is wrong and the executor compensates by re-checking every candidate against the heap — which is what `Heap Fetches` counts

An index-only scan may skip the heap only for rows whose heap page is marked all-visible in the visibility map; only VACUUM sets that bit and any write to the page clears it. The staging copy was vacuumed once and never written again, so every bit was set. On the churning production table few pages are all-visible, so almost every row pays a heap fetch plus a visibility check, and the scan has quietly degraded into an ordinary index scan
explanation: Visibility information lives only in heap tuple headers — an index entry is key plus TID and knows nothing about transactions — so on the face of it an index can never answer a query alone. The visibility map is the workaround: one bit per heap page meaning 'every tuple here is visible to everyone', small enough to stay cached, so visibility becomes a page-level question answerable without reading the page. The consequence is the one biting here: an index-only scan is fast in exact proportion to how recently the table was vacuumed, because only VACUUM sets bits and any write clears them. A restored, never-written staging copy is the best case that can possibly exist and is therefore a misleading benchmark for this plan shape; `Heap Fetches` is the metric that exposes the difference. The levers are all on the churn-and-vacuum side — more aggressive autovacuum on that table, or fewer page-clearing writes (a lower `fillfactor` keeping updates HOT and page-local) — not on the index definition, which is already correct. The distractors each borrow a real mechanism: suffix truncation applies to separator keys in internal pages, a fan-out optimisation that never touches leaf payload, and INCLUDE columns live in the leaves precisely so index-only scans can return them; index bloat does add descent reads, but those are reported as buffer counts, not `Heap Fetches`; and stale statistics influence which plan is chosen, not how many heap trips a chosen index-only scan makes.

question: `orders` is queried almost exclusively by `WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'shipped' AND created_at >= $2 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20`, and only a few percent of any tenant's rows are `shipped`. Which index shape should the team create, and on what reasoning?
choices: `(created_at, tenant_id, status)` — leading with the column that carries both the range predicate and the ORDER BY lets a single descent bound the scan and emit rows already sorted, after which the two equality columns filter inside that range

`(tenant_id, status, created_at)` — the equality columns come first, so the descent lands on exactly this tenant's shipped rows; and because `created_at` is the next column, entries inside that range are already in `created_at` order, so the backward walk emits sorted rows and stops after 20
Either ordering performs the same. The descent range is determined by the set of predicates rather than by column order, and the planner reorders index columns when it matches them to a query

Two single-column indexes, on `tenant_id` and on `status`, combined by a BitmapAnd — strictly more flexible than one composite index, and the `ORDER BY … LIMIT` is satisfied straight from the bitmap in index order
explanation: A multicolumn index sorts like a phone book: by the first column, then by the second within equal firsts, and so on. Equality predicates on the leading columns plus the first inequality are what bound the descent; every predicate after that inequality can only filter rows already being walked. `(tenant_id, status, created_at)` therefore turns all three predicates into one tight contiguous range, and — because `created_at` is the last key, sorted inside each `(tenant_id, status)` group — the leaf walk emits exactly the requested order, so the left-links serve the DESC scan and the LIMIT stops after twenty entries with no Sort node. Reversing to `(created_at, tenant_id, status)` still gives sorted output, which is what makes it tempting, but the range on `created_at` becomes the bound: the scan walks every tenant's rows in the whole time window and discards the ones that do not match, so its cost grows with total traffic rather than with this tenant's shipped orders — and with only a few percent matching, the LIMIT has to chew through a great deal before it finds twenty. The rule of thumb falls straight out of the structure: equality columns first, the inequality and ORDER BY column last. Column order is not something the planner can paper over — skip scan only fakes a *missing leading* column when it has few distinct values, by internally re-running the descent once per value, which is not the same as reordering keys. And the two-index bitmap path loses the property the query depends on: a bitmap is built in heap-page order, so ordering is gone, a Sort reappears, the LIMIT can no longer stop early, and the plan pays heap fetches that a single ordered index scan avoids.

question: A 2 TB append-only telemetry table is inserted strictly in `occurred_at` order. Two access paths matter: a nightly aggregate over a one-day range, and a live dashboard running `ORDER BY occurred_at DESC LIMIT 50`. To reclaim the 40 GB the `btree (occurred_at)` occupies, a developer proposes replacing it with `brin (occurred_at)`. What is the right call?
choices: Replace it. BRIN summarises block ranges in physical order, so a backward BRIN scan returns rows newest-first and the dashboard's LIMIT still stops after 50, while the aggregate gets the same block skipping for a fraction of the space

Keep the btree, because BRIN pays the same MVCC tax that made the btree large — one entry per row version plus dead entries awaiting VACUUM — so the space saving evaporates as soon as the table starts seeing updates

Split the decision by access path. BRIN is right for the day-range aggregate: a min/max summary per range of heap blocks, resting on the heap's physical correlation with `occurred_at`, skips nearly every block at a tiny fraction of the size. It is wrong for the dashboard: with no per-row entries and no key ordering it cannot emit rows in `occurred_at` order, so `ORDER BY … LIMIT 50` becomes a scan of all candidate blocks plus a Sort. Keep a btree if that path matters — and note that the whole BRIN premise is physical correlation, which a later backfill or a non-HOT update pattern can quietly destroy
Replace the btree with `hash (occurred_at)` instead: it stores only the hash so it is smaller than either alternative, and its bucket chains serve both the day range and the ordered LIMIT
explanation: Core PostgreSQL asks an access method for very little — map keys to TIDs, one entry per row version, cooperate with VACUUM — and leaves the internals to the AM, which is why choosing one is a question about what the data physically looks like and what the query needs back. BRIN keeps no per-row entries at all, only a min/max summary per range of heap blocks, which is what makes it minuscule and also what caps what it can answer: it narrows a scan to candidate blocks, and it can do that only while the heap's physical order tracks the column. That fits the day-range aggregate perfectly. It does not fit the dashboard, because ordering is a property of ordered access methods; BRIN has no sorted key space to walk, so the planner must gather every candidate block and sort, and a LIMIT cannot stop early. The correlation premise also deserves an explicit warning rather than an assumption: it is a property of insert order, and a backfill of older rows or an update pattern that relocates versions to fresh pages degrades it silently, with no error and no plan change — just a BRIN scan that stops skipping. The distractors each invert something structural: BRIN's block ranges being in physical order is not key ordering and does not produce sorted output; it is a summarizing index, which is exactly why it does *not* get one entry per row version and why it does not disqualify HOT updates — the opposite of the claim in the second option; and hashing destroys order by construction, so a hash index answers `=` and nothing else, neither a range nor a sort.
